rubric.naPolicy: Dimensions 4 (Constraint Explicitness), 5 (Success Measurability) and 6 (Competitive Positioning) are meta-layer dimensions owned by meta/constraints.md, meta/problem-statement.md and meta/competitive-landscape.md. They are scored N/A for every unit inside this domain except the domain root, where the index's 'Why this is a top-level domain' section is itself an explicit competitive argument naming competitors and a moat mechanism, so dimension 6 is scored.

units.notes: Dimension 3 ❌ for two silent contradictions carried in this unit's own files (k-anonymity on the demand map; vault-lapse locking). Dimension 7 ✅ — Q-01..Q-10 all carry an owner and either a deferral stage or a cited resolution. Dimension 8 ⚠️ for the CX confidence-count mismatch.

Exceptionally deep on 20.01.01/.02/.03 (concurrency, race, malicious-input, multi-hyphenate rows all present with specified outcomes). ⚠️ on 3 for the artist per-fan consent-visibility conflict; ⚠️ on 7 for five ownerless [PENDING — /ideate-discover Step 5 deepening] markers pointing at a stage that has already run.

CX-04 (live segment vs snapshot entitlement) is the model of a well-resolved tension. ⚠️ on 3 for a wrong owning-domain pointer on the Membership dimension and the blocked-vs-first-come over-promise gate; ⚠️ on 7 for bare [PENDING] cells that same-file decisions already answer.

❌ on 3: the per-fan frequency cap is consumed as a dispatch gate with a concrete user-visible outcome, but its named owner specifies nothing. ⚠️ on 7 for two ownerless Step-5 PENDINGs in the CX, one of which a child has since resolved.

The deepest unit in the domain — typed product kinds, error codes, hold windows, arithmetic-checked happy path (15 − 1 − 1.40 = 12.60; 70/20/10 = 8.82/2.52/1.26 all correct). ❌ on 3 for the authorization-vs-settlement split-version binding conflict on a money path. ⚠️ on 7 for a stale CX PENDING its own child resolved and a deferral pointed at an audit-queue id with no owner or stage.

Cleanest tracking in the domain: every inline PENDING names either an [OWNER] call plus a stage, or its own Q row which carries owner + stage. ⚠️ on 3 for the membership physical-benefit publish gate routed to a file that does not specify it.

The radius conflict (25 mi vs 80 km) is NOT reported — it is explicitly recorded in 20.06.02 D-06 and Q-04 with [OWNER] and /create-prd, which is the documented mechanism working. ❌ on 3 for the re-download format contradiction with 20.04.03. ⚠️ on 7 for the duplicate Q-04 id.

findings.claim: Download re-download rights are specified two incompatible ways: 20.04.03 makes the entitlement format-agnostic (buy once, download any offered format forever) and explicitly rejects the alternative, while 20.06.03 restricts re-download to the formats actually purchased.
findings.evidence: 20.04.03-digital-sales-name-your-price-bundles.md:69-70 — "the entitlement is format-agnostic (one purchase entitles all offered formats — you bought the record, not a file), and re-downloading in a different format later is free and unlimited"; D-08 (line 161) — "Download entitlement is format-agnostic and never expires | See DT-05. Buy the record, not a file; re-download any offered format forever"; DT-05 (line 130) — "❌ REJECTED — the fan buys the record, not a file. Binding the entitlement to a single format re-download is a streaming-era mistake: it means a fan who bought MP3 in 2026 and wants FLAC in 2029 has to re-buy." AGAINST: 20.06.03-fan-library-collection.md:67-68 — "Download: the fan re-downloads the original purchased formats (e.g. FLAC, WAV, MP3-320, ALAC — whatever the release offered and they bought)"; :24 Role Lens Fan — "re-downloads in the format purchased"; D-01 (line 168) — "re-downloadable indefinitely, in the purchased formats, with no expiry or count cap".
findings.forcedInvention: Whether the library exposes a format selector for an owned release or only the format(s) bought. The exact scenario 20.04.03 DT-05 calls a mistake (bought MP3 in 2026, wants FLAC in 2029) is the behaviour 20.06.03 specifies, and nothing marks either statement as provisional.
findings.failureScenario: Fan buys an album as MP3-320 in 2026. In 2029 they open the library on a new laptop and want the FLAC. Implementer A (reading 20.04.03 D-08) offers all offered formats free. Implementer B (reading 20.06.03 D-01 and its Role Lens) offers MP3-320 only and the fan must re-buy — which 20.04.03 DT-05 states is the failure the design exists to prevent.

findings.claim: The payout-plan version that governs a sale is bound at two different payment-lifecycle events in two files dated the same day: at payment settlement in 20.04.03 and at payment authorization in 20.04.04.
findings.evidence: 20.04.03-digital-sales-name-your-price-bundles.md:108 — "Split changes between add-to-cart and settlement (a dispute resolves mid-checkout) | The payout plan version is bound at payment settlement, not at add-to-cart, and the entitlement records that version." AGAINST: 20.04.04-d2f-revenue-split-payout.md:99 — "Split applied at payment authorization against the plan version live at that instant"; :115 — "Each sale is locked to the split version live at the moment it is authorized — a domain 09 edit mid-checkout does not re-bind an in-flight sale"; :121 — "A late confirmation carrying a superseded plan version does not re-bind the sale; the accrual applies the split version that was live when the sale was authorized." 20.04.04 also mixes the two internally: :44 has shares accruing "the moment the sale clears" while :99 binds at authorization.
findings.forcedInvention: Which payment event stamps the plan version. Authorization and settlement/capture are distinct events separated by hours or days, and domain 09 splits are editable in between (both files specify a mid-checkout dispute resolution as a live scenario).
findings.failureScenario: A fan authorizes a £15 NYP purchase at 09:00. At 11:00 a domain 09 dispute resolves and the drummer's share moves from 10% to 20%. Capture settles at 14:00. Under 20.04.04 the drummer is paid £1.26 (10%, the authorization-time version); under 20.04.03 the drummer is paid £2.52 (20%, the settlement-time version). Both files claim to specify the payout of the same sale, and the payee statement names a plan version that differs by implementation.

findings.claim: The demand map is specified as both floored and unfloored for k-anonymity: 20.07 makes a k-anonymity floor on the map a locked decision, while the domain CX and 20.02.01 both state that aggregate/counting surfaces are explicitly not floored.
findings.evidence: 20.07-fan-demand-show-requests.md:110 D-05 — "k-anonymity floor on the map | '3 fans in Inverness' names people. The floor belongs on the map, not on the fan record"; :69 edge case — "k-anonymity floor on the map, not on the fan record. Ties to 20.02.01 DT-03." AGAINST: fanbase-direct-to-fan-cx.md:255 CX-10 §3 — "Individually-targeted reads inherit the k-anonymity floor (domain 24); aggregate geo-density is unfloored map data"; :55 CX-01 §3 — "counting/record-view is unfloored, but individually-targeted send/export is floored by the k-anonymity rule escalated to domain 24"; 20.02.01-segment-builder.md:99 DT-03 — "My read: the floor belongs on send and on export, not on counting or record viewing."
findings.forcedInvention: Whether the demand map suppresses sub-k clusters. 20.07 cites 20.02.01 DT-03 as its authority, but DT-03 says the opposite of what 20.07 D-05 concludes: the map is a counting/aggregate surface, which DT-03 and both CX rows place outside the floor. No marker flags the disagreement on either side.
findings.failureScenario: Artist opens the demand map for Scotland with 3 fans in Inverness. Implementer A (20.07 D-05) suppresses the Inverness cluster or rolls it into a region, so the artist cannot see demand exists there — the edge case 'Demand exists where the artist cannot economically play' says show it because 'it is still true'. Implementer B (CX-10 §3) renders '3 fans in Inverness', which 20.07 says 'is close to naming them, and it is a real disclosure of a person's location to an artist'. One implementation leaks; the other withholds the signal the feature exists to give.

findings.claim: Membership lapse is specified with opposite interim defaults: the domain CX requires member-gated vault rows to lock immediately and fail closed to locked, while both 20.05.02 and 20.06.03 specify that items the fan had while entitled stay accessible.
findings.evidence: fanbase-direct-to-fan-cx.md:340-341 CX-14 — "Membership-gated vault items lock the instant a membership lapses, and that lock is felt in the fan's library"; :356 §2 — "Must be atomic-enough that the library never shows a stale unlocked state after a lapse — fail-closed to locked on ambiguity"; :359 §5 — "Resolution: fail closed to locked". AGAINST: 20.05.02-exclusive-content-vault.md:73 — "until ratified, the safe default is no retroactive removal (matches D-05); items opened while entitled stay accessible"; 20.05.01-membership-tiers-benefits.md:78 — "a lapsed fan keeps what they opened and loses only future items"; 20.06.03-fan-library-collection.md:114 — "on lapse, per 20.05.02 DT-02's leaning, items released while the fan was paying stay accessible and future items lock."
findings.forcedInvention: What the library shows for a vault item the fan opened while paying, the moment their membership lapses. CX-14 scopes the tracked open question narrowly to 'whether previously downloaded copies survive' while itself asserting the row locks; the three feature files assert access persists. Both are written as the shipping interim behaviour pending 20.05.02 Q-01.
findings.failureScenario: A fan's card fails, dunning expires, membership lapses. They open their library and click a demo they played last month. Implementer A (CX-14) shows it locked and fails closed — the outcome 20.05.02 says 'feels like theft' and D-05 forbids. Implementer B (20.05.02/20.06.03) plays it. The keep-vs-lose ruling is legitimately deferred, but the two files disagree about what ships until it lands.

findings.claim: 20.03.03 specifies a per-fan frequency cap as a mandatory dispatch gate with concrete user-visible behaviour and names 20.02 as its owner, but no file in 20.02 — index, CX, or any of its three features — mentions frequency capping at all, so the policy exists nowhere.
findings.evidence: 20.03.03-send-scheduling-throttling.md:61 — "Two campaigns scheduled to overlapping segments in the same window | Both would buzz the same fan. A per-fan frequency cap (owned outside this node) governs: the second message is deferred or suppressed for the overlapping fans... | '1,090 fans already got a message today — deferred for them.'"; :93 Cross-Cut Notes — "Gated by per-fan frequency capping (owned in 20.02 Segmentation & Superfan Intelligence) — this node checks the cap at dispatch and defers/suppresses over-limit fans (DT-04); it does not set the cap. `-cx.md` frequency-fatigue thread."; :107 D-08 — "Frequency capping is a separate policy this node consumes, not owns." A grep for 'frequency cap|frequency capping|frequency budget|fan-fatigue|fatigue' across all 41 files of domain 20 returns hits only in 20.03.03 (4) and in 20.01.03:61 ("the tier's frequency cap" — the fan-chosen tier cap, e.g. Highlights ≤1/month, a different object from DT-04's artist-blind per-fan budget). 20.03-broadcast-fan-messaging-cx.md contains no frequency-fatigue thread (CX-01..CX-05 only).
findings.forcedInvention: The entire cap policy: the window (the quoted copy implies per-day, while the only cap that does exist — 20.01.03's Highlights tier — is per-calendar-month), the limit, whether over-limit fans are deferred or suppressed, and who sets it. DT-04 states the cap is 'a per-fan, per-artist budget' distinct from the fan's own tier choice, so 20.01.03's tiers cannot supply it.
findings.failureScenario: An artist sends a tour announcement at 10:00 and a merch drop at 16:00 to overlapping segments. The dispatcher must consult a cap to decide whether the 1,090 overlapping fans get the second message. There is no specified cap, so the implementer invents one (or ships no cap, silently deleting the gate D-08 declares mandatory and letting a warm sender both send fast and send often — the exact outcome DT-04 says the split exists to prevent).

findings.claim: Whether an artist can see an individual fan's unsubscribe/preference history is specified both ways: 20.01.02 grants the Musician a full per-fan grant/revoke evidence chain, while 20.01.03 states the artist sees churn only in aggregate and cannot see who rejected what.
findings.evidence: 20.01.02-consent-legal-basis.md:23 Role Lens Musician — "Can open any single fan's evidence chain (every grant/revoke event: timestamp, owning entity, channel, purpose, exact wording shown, source surface, provenance strength, captured IP/user-agent where the platform witnessed it)." AGAINST: 20.01.03-fan-preference-centre.md:24 Role Lens Musician — "Has no write path and no per-fan toggle history as an editable object. Cannot re-subscribe, cannot restore, cannot see a per-fan feed of who rejected what — only the roll-up"; D-04 (line 162) — "Artists have no write path and see churn only in aggregate | Per-fan unsubscribe feeds train artists to take it personally." The two are the same data: 20.01.03:36 — "Every control is a consent-ledger event, never an in-place settings update", so every tier change, channel mute and unsubscribe made in the Preference Centre is an event in the chain 20.01.02 lets the artist open.
findings.forcedInvention: Whether the fan-record UI shows 'unsubscribed 14 Mar via preference centre' per fan. 20.01.03's carve-outs ('as an editable object', 'a per-fan feed') can be read as barring only a stream and an edit surface, but D-04's 'see churn only in aggregate' is unqualified and covers on-demand lookup too.
findings.failureScenario: Artist opens a fan's record after a campaign. Implementer A (20.01.02) renders the full evidence chain including the unsubscribe, its timestamp and the wording shown. Implementer B (20.01.03 D-04) renders no per-fan consent history and only an aggregate churn number. The complaint-defence use case 20.01.02 specifies ('Consent evidence requested during a spam complaint') needs A; the anti-resentment design D-04 specifies needs B.

findings.claim: 20.01.04 leaves the stale-consent import case as an unowned [PENDING] pointed at a stage that has already run, when 20.01.02 — the authoritative owner of consent — has already fixed the default.
findings.evidence: 20.01.04-fan-list-import-hygiene.md:57 — "Import of 200k rows from a venue's decade-old box office | Volume is fine; the consent age is not. `[PENDING — /ideate-discover Step 5 deepening]` on whether stale consent (Q-02 on 20.01.02) blocks. | `[PENDING]`" — no owner, and the deferral target is the breadth/deepening stage that produced the [DEEP] status on 20.01.01/.02/.03 and this file's own [PARTIAL]. AGAINST: 20.01.02-consent-legal-basis.md:84 — "Consent granted 24+ months ago, fan never engaged | Consent does not auto-expire... The platform surfaces a staleness advisory... and downgrades that fan's deliverability tier, but blocks no send on age alone"; Q-02 (line 154) — "Default is fixed (consent never auto-expires; staleness ≥24 months is surfaced and deliverability-downgraded but blocks no send, per the edge-case table)."
findings.forcedInvention: What the venue sees when importing a decade-old 200k-row list — the 'User Sees' cell is literally `[PENDING]`, so the implementer must invent the whole surface, even though the governing rule (import completes, records land in the artist-asserted deliverability-downgraded tier, nothing is blocked on age) is already settled two files away.
findings.failureScenario: An implementer building the import breakdown screen for a venue's 200k-row box-office export finds a [PENDING] cell where the outcome copy belongs, and a deferral pointed at a completed stage with no owner to ask. They either invent a block (contradicting 20.01.02's fixed default) or ship no message about consent age at all.

findings.claim: The 20.01 CX file carries four [PENDING — /ideate-discover Step 5 deepening] markers with no owner, aimed at a stage that has completed; three of the four have since been answered by the children, so the CX presents settled behaviour as open.
findings.evidence: 20.01-fan-graph-owned-audience-cx.md:41 — "Import permission does not confer send permission. `[PENDING — /ideate-discover Step 5 deepening]` on whether weak-provenance records are sendable-with-warning or hard-blocked until re-permissioned" (answered: 20.01.02:88 — records "land in the artist-asserted (unmarketable-until-re-permissioned) tier"; 20.01.04 D-03 — "Unanswered provenance imports data anyway, into an unmarketable tier"); :42 — "whether a re-permission campaign to imported records is itself lawful... `[PENDING — /ideate-discover Step 5 deepening]`" (properly tracked elsewhere as 20.01.04 Q-01, User, /create-prd-security); :64 — "A merge must not fan out to the fan... `[PENDING — /ideate-discover Step 5 deepening]`" (answered: 20.01.01:25 — "a merge is silent to the fan (CX-02)"); :104 — "Merge strategy on a contested split is `[PENDING — /ideate-discover Step 5 deepening]`; the plausible options are unanimous-consent, majority-of-members, or fork-with-notice" (properly tracked as 20.01.05 Q-02, User, /create-prd). None of the four names an owner.
findings.forcedInvention: Nothing product-level for three of them, but a reader who consults the CX file for the synthesis answers — which is what it is for — is told four decisions are open when three are closed, and has no owner to route the fourth to.
findings.failureScenario: A downstream stage reads the 20.01 CX synthesis to build the import→consent trigger chain and treats weak-provenance sendability as undecided, re-litigating a rule 20.01.02 D-08 and 20.01.04 D-03 have already fixed, or ships a merge notification to the fan that 20.01.01 explicitly forbids.

findings.claim: The segment builder's Membership dimension names 20.04 (Direct-to-Fan Storefront) as its source domain; membership state is owned by 20.05.01, as the sibling file correctly records.
findings.evidence: 20.02.01-segment-builder.md:44 — "| **Membership** | tier / joined-since date / active vs lapsed (no activity in N days) | 20.04 |". AGAINST: 20.02.02-superfan-score.md:34 — "| Membership tenure / active tier | Recurring commitment. | 20.05.01 |"; fanbase-direct-to-fan-cx.md:183 CX-07 §1 — "Membership state is owned by 20.05.01 (billing engine is CX-M24); the score reads it"; 20.05-memberships-patronage-campaigns-index.md:26 lists 20.05.01 Membership Tiers & Benefits as the tier owner. 20.04's own Role Matrix (20.04-direct-to-fan-storefront-index.md:46-49) contains no membership child.
findings.forcedInvention: Where the builder reads tier/joined-since/active-vs-lapsed from. An implementer following the table goes to the storefront, which holds no membership state at all (its only membership-adjacent concept is the `members-item` gate flag, which resolves through 20.02.03).
findings.failureScenario: Implementer wires the Membership segment family against 20.04's catalogue and finds no tier or tenure field, then either invents one in the storefront (duplicating 20.05.01's state, which CX-07 forbids since 'the score never writes membership') or stalls.

findings.claim: 20.02.02 leaves two edge-case outcomes as bare [PENDING] with no owner and no deferral target, although that same file's decision table already fixes both.
findings.evidence: 20.02.02-superfan-score.md:72 — "New artist, no purchase/scan history | Score degrades to open/click — i.e. to Mailchimp... | `[PENDING]` — the honest answer may be to withhold scoring until there is signal, rather than show a confident number built on nothing" — but D-04 (line 117) states it flatly: "Withhold the score rather than show a low-confidence one | Cold-start (DT-02). An artist who trusts a fabricated rank makes worse decisions than one who knows they lack data." And :73 — "Wealthy fan vs devoted broke fan | Spend-weighted scoring ranks a rich casual above a devoted teenager who came to nine shows on a bus... | `[PENDING]`" — but D-01 (line 114) states it: "Attendance (scans) outweighs spend." Neither [PENDING] carries an owner or a stage.
findings.forcedInvention: What the artist sees in the cold-start and spend-vs-devotion cases. The behaviour is decided; only the surface copy is missing, and the bare marker gives no owner or stage to obtain it from — while wrongly signalling that the underlying policy is still open.
findings.failureScenario: An implementer reading the edge-case table treats cold-start scoring as an unresolved policy and ships a low-confidence numeric score for a new artist — the precise outcome D-04 exists to forbid ('a confident-looking wrong number is worse than an honest gap').

findings.claim: Over-promising a presale is specified as blocked at grant time, but the specified user-facing remedy offers a path that proceeds with a first-come disclosure — so the grant is both refused and permitted.
findings.evidence: 20.02.03-perk-entitlements-presale-eligibility.md:96 D-03 — "Over-promise is blocked at grant time | See DT-02. Disappointing your best fans is the worst outcome this feature can produce, and it is entirely preventable." AGAINST the same file's :54 edge case — "Presale allocation smaller than the eligible set | ... Must be caught at grant time, not at on-sale. | 'You're promising 1,203 fans access to 300 tickets. Narrow the audience, or say plainly that it's first-come.'" DT-02 (:76) says the check "must be blunt rather than a warning nobody reads" without saying whether blunt means refusing.
findings.forcedInvention: Whether an over-subscribed presale can be granted at all. 'Blocked' and 'or say plainly that it's first-come' cannot both hold: the second is a way of proceeding.
findings.failureScenario: Artist grants a 48-hour presale to 1,203 eligible fans against 300 tickets. Implementer A disables the grant until the audience is narrowed. Implementer B shows a modal with a 'label it first-come' option and arms the presale for 1,203 fans, producing the 903 disappointed superfans DT-02 identifies as the feature's worst outcome.

findings.claim: 20.03.02's Behavior section and DT-02 assert that the platform has one web surface with mobile unresolved, and conclude push is unusable — a premise the same file's own Q-04 records as superseded by a ratified decision that puts PWA web push in v1.
findings.evidence: 20.03.02-channel-routing-bulk-delivery.md:40-44 — "Push is only available where the fan has an app — and `meta/constraints.md` declares web as the only surface, with mobile an open question. Web push exists but is weak on iOS. This means push is, today, a channel this domain mostly cannot use"; DT-02 (:85) — "`meta/constraints.md` declares one responsive web surface; mobile is an open question." AGAINST the same file's Q-04 (:119) — "RESOLVED — ... `meta/constraints.md` § Project Surfaces now declares Mobile (PWA) in v1 ('web is installable as a PWA (home-screen, web push for gig alerts…)')... Ratified as ideation-index D-28... So push is not lost: it arrives in v1 as PWA web push." Neither the Behavior paragraph nor the channel table (:38, Push) is annotated as superseded, unlike the domain index, which does annotate its own stale gate at fanbase-direct-to-fan-index.md:15-18 ("Gate superseded (2026-07-16)").
findings.forcedInvention: Whether the broadcast dispatcher implements a push leg in v1. The Behavior text says the channel mostly cannot be used; Q-04 says it ships as PWA web push with a documented iOS home-screen caveat.
findings.failureScenario: Implementer builds channel routing from the Behavior section and channel table, ships email and SMS only, and treats push as out of scope. 20.05.06 then depends on a go-live push and 20.06.02 D-06 defaults every follow to geo-gated alerts whose v1 channel is exactly that PWA push.

findings.claim: `members-item` appears as a row in the product-kind table under the rule that a product declares exactly one kind, while the prose immediately below states it is not a kind but a visibility flag — and miscounts the table while doing so.
findings.evidence: 20.04.01-storefront-product-catalog.md:34 — "A product declares exactly one **kind**"; the table at :38-45 lists six kinds, the sixth being "| `members-item` | Any of the above, gated | As underlying kind | 20.02.03 | As underlying kind |". AGAINST :52-53 — "`members-item` is a **gate flag** on any other kind, not a seventh kind — a members-only download is a `digital-download` with `visibility = members` and an entitlement requirement (20.02.03)." The table has six rows, so members-item would be the sixth, not the seventh — evidence the two were never reconciled.
findings.forcedInvention: Whether `members-item` is a value of the `kind` enum or a `visibility` field. The prose gives the answer, but the table (which the publish-time kind validation and the Operator kind restriction at :54 both key on) contradicts it.
findings.failureScenario: Implementer adds `members-item` to the kind enum from the table. A members-only download now has kind `members-item`, so the kind-based delegation at :40 (digital detail → 20.04.03) and the Operator restriction ('Operators may only create merch-pod, merch-stocked, and their bundles thereof') no longer resolve — a members-only venue tote is either rejected or silently permitted depending on which rule wins.

findings.claim: The 10% rolling reserve is described as taken from each disbursement in the parameter table and from each accrual in the happy path, which changes the balance the payee sees.
findings.evidence: 20.04.04-d2f-revenue-split-payout.md:58 — "| **Rolling reserve** | **10%** of each disbursement held **90 days**, released if no refund/chargeback/dispute touches the originating sale |". AGAINST :99 happy path step 5 — "artist £8.82, producer £2.52, drummer £1.26 — each accrues immediately, each with a 10% reserve held for 90 days"; and Role Lens :29 — "Sees per sale where the money went: gross, platform cut, each payee's share, the 10% rolling reserve held" (per sale, i.e. at accrual).
findings.forcedInvention: Whether the reserve is withheld when a share accrues (so the drummer's visible balance is £1.13, not £1.26, and the £20 disbursement threshold is measured against the reduced figure) or when a disbursement is cut (balance shows £1.26 and 10% is held back at payout).
findings.failureScenario: Drummer accrues £1.26 on a sale. Implementer A shows £1.13 available plus £0.13 reserved and needs £20 of net accrual to trigger a payout; Implementer B shows £1.26 accrued, triggers at £20 gross and holds £2 back at disbursement. The refund cover order ('reversed against each payee's rolling reserve pro-rata first') behaves differently for a refund landing before any disbursement, because under A a reserve exists and under B it does not.

findings.claim: The fund-segregation policy for money-now-object-later sales is scoped to pre-order *bundles* everywhere it is stated, leaving a standalone physical-record pre-order — which the catalogue explicitly supports via the `presale` price rule — with no segregation requirement, the exact routing-around the domain CX warns of.
findings.evidence: 20.04.01-storefront-product-catalog.md:43 — "| `physical-record` (vinyl/CD) | Held/pressed stock, ships | Finite; **pre-order window allowed** |"; :66 — "| `presale` | underlying rule + `release_at`, optional `presale_amount` | ... **charged now, fulfilled at/after `release_at`** |" — neither mentions fund segregation, and 20.04.02 (which owns physical-record detail per the taxonomy) never mentions it either. The policy is bundle-scoped in every statement: 20.04.03 D-03 (:156) — "**Pre-order bundles** carry the same fund-segregation policy as crowdfunding"; 20.05 index D-03 (:60) — "Pre-order **bundles** in 20.04.03 fall under the same fund policy as crowdfunding"; 20.05.05:92 — "Same policy applies to pre-order **bundles** in 20.04.03". The hazard is named in fanbase-direct-to-fan-cx.md:321 CX-13 — "If the fund-segregation policy (20.05 D-02) applies to one and not the other, artists will route around it by calling every campaign a pre-order."
findings.forcedInvention: Whether money taken on a standalone vinyl pre-order (physical-record + presale price rule, no digital component, so not a bundle) is segregated. Every statement of the policy names bundles; no file extends it to the bare presale rule.
findings.failureScenario: Artist lists a `physical-record` with a `presale` rule, charged now for a March pressing, no digital component. Implementer follows 20.04.01's presale rule literally, settles the money to the artist's balance immediately, and the £9,000 taken for an unpressed record is spendable — the PledgeMusic failure 20.05 D-02 exists to prevent, reached by taking the one door nobody wrote the policy on.

findings.claim: The permission conjunct required to publish a digital-download or NYP bundle is left unresolved with no owner and no pipeline stage — the deferral points only at an audit-queue identifier.
findings.evidence: 20.04.01-storefront-product-catalog.md:185 — "Touches 01 Identity, Profiles & Organizations — *permission, currently unstated*. Publishing a product for an artist entity is one party acting for another and needs both of `01.03.02` D-05's conjuncts: the `list` activity, plus `merch` in the edge's `domains` for merch kinds. On a membership edge the domain conjunct is universal. Which domain a digital download or an NYP bundle sells into is not settled — it is the open taxonomy question recorded against DQ-R2-01, not a call this feature may make." No owner, no `/create-prd*` stage, and no row in this file's Open Questions table (Q-01..Q-04 cover rights records, guest checkout, physical records, and venue merch — none of them this).
findings.forcedInvention: The domain value a delegate's representation edge must carry to publish a digital download, and therefore whether a manager with a signed mandate can list a record at all. The file forbids itself from deciding and points at no stage that will.
findings.failureScenario: Implementer wires the publish permission check for `digital-download`. The merch conjunct is specified ('merch' in the edge's domains); the digital one is not, and the pointer resolves to an audit-queue id rather than a pipeline stage. They either invent a domain value, or block delegate publishing of every digital product — silently narrowing what a managed artist can sell.
